1	# Issue #230 facts: a web control surface on the remote port
2	
3	There was no spike. The tree and primary sources settle everything that
4	can be checked here. What is left needs a real browser on a device and
5	a person's tap through the certificate warning. Safari is the only
6	browser on this Mac, and driving it needs `safaridriver --enable`, an
7	admin step, so none of it runs here. Line numbers are at 7fe8949.
8	
9	## Settled
10	
11	### The tree
12	
13	- `RemoteRequest` is built in one place, `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:506`). Nothing in `tests/`, `control/` or `client/` names `RemoteRequest` or `RemoteReply` (grep), because `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP. A new request field (cookie, origin, user agent, subprotocol) touches one constructor. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteRequest {"` gives only `src/adapters/remote.rs:506`.
14	- `RemoteReply { status, body, authenticated }` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:389-393`) is built literally 28 times in `src/app.rs` and twice in `src/adapters/remote.rs`. A headers field needs a `Default` or a constructor, or all 30 sites change. Evidence: `grep -c "RemoteReply {"`.
15	- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` are in `src/adapters/`, not in `ports/`, `model.rs` or `action.rs`, so CLAUDE.md's additive-contract rule ("`src/core/model.rs`, `src/core/action.rs` … and `src/ports/` are the shared contract") does not cover them. Evidence: CLAUDE.md "Extending the contract"; `src/adapters/remote.rs:360,389`.
16	- The certificate can be reissued over the existing key without changing `spki_sha256`. The SPKI hash is computed from the key alone (`spki_sha256_of_key`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:138-141`), and rcgen signs any params with a loaded key (`KeyPair::from_pem`, `:139,146`; `CertificateParams::self_signed(&self, signing_key)`, rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:154`). `make_identity` always generates a new key (`src/adapters/remote.rs:105`), so a reissue is a new function.
17	- rcgen 0.14 can carry what a browser or an installed trust needs: `subject_alt_names` with `SanType::IpAddress` and DNS names, `extended_key_usages` with `ServerAuth`, `not_before`/`not_after` and `is_ca`. Evidence: rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:57-64,755,812`; `src/lib.rs:313`.
18	- rcgen's default validity is notBefore 1975-01-01 to notAfter 4096-01-01, and the current certificate takes both. Evidence: rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:83-84`; `src/adapters/remote.rs:106` (`CertificateParams::new` with no override).
19	- The current certificate has no subjectAltName, only a CN, and no EKU. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:106-111`.
20	- `local_address()` always returns IPv4. It binds `0.0.0.0` and connects to `192.0.2.1`, so a URL built from it never needs IPv6 brackets. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`.
21	- The Bonjour host name is `<hostname -s>.local.` as registered by `mdns-sd` (`src/adapters/bonjour.rs:41-48`, `default_server_name` `src/adapters/remote.rs:304-313`). Whether that matches macOS's own LocalHostName is not checked here (Unresolved).
22	- A code is single use: the first pairing closes the window. The window also closes after three failures or five minutes. A code left in browser history is dead once used or expired. Evidence: `src/core/remote.rs:46-69` (`Paired` sets `self.pairing = None`).
23	- The record carries no `last_message`. It exists only on the hook event (`src/ports/events.rs:24`, `src/adapters/hooks.rs:71,196`) and is not on `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`). The card's excerpt is computed in the UI from the transcript for agents (`agent_excerpt`, `src/ui/cards.rs:176-178,558`) and from the pane caption or host title for the other kinds (`src/ui/cards.rs:179-184`). An excerpt on the wire is therefore new work, not a field to expose.
24	- The watch set is global across the port, capped at 128, least recently read evicted silently. A page that watches one key per listed session can push a headset's keys out. The headset loses only the `changed` events until its next read. Evidence: `docs/remote-client.md:131,254,543`.
25	- The spec forbids the token in a URL: "sent only as a bearer header … never in a URL" (`docs/remote-client.md:312`) and "keep tokens out of logs, URLs" (`:318`). Both lines name the bearer header, so either cookie or subprotocol transport amends `:312`.
26	- §5's claim that "a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails" (`docs/remote-client.md:309`) rests on the client sending the `spki_sha256` it saw on the wire. The host checks only what the body says (`remote_pair`, `src/app.rs:3639-3647`), so the claim holds only for a client that can read its own connection's certificate (whether any browser API exposes it: Unresolved).
27	- The pairing token is base64url with no padding, 43 characters (`src/adapters/remote.rs:340`; `docs/remote-client.md:312`). Its characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _` are all RFC 7230 `tchar`, so it is a valid `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230#section-3.2.6 (tchar includes `-` and `_`).
28	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114-116`). It is called by `switchboard-remote` (`main.swift:111`) and `BrowserView` (`:106` for a pasted line, `:883`). `ConnectionManager` builds one (`:474`) and uses `invite.addresses.compactMap(Address.init).first` (`:483`), so only the first address is used and a one-element list from a URL is enough. Eight test files under `client/Tests` name `PairingInvite`.
29	
30	### Browsers and platforms
31	
32	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` takes no headers. The handshake is a Fetch with credentials mode `"include"`, so the browser's cookies for the URL go with it. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ ("credentials mode … include"; constructor signature).
33	- If the page passes a subprotocol and the 101 response does not echo one of them, the browser fails the connection. The host must therefore write `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` in `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) if the token travels that way. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (opening handshake: "covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server").
34	- Secure contexts are decided by scheme alone: an `https`/`wss` origin is "potentially trustworthy" whatever the certificate's state. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ ("Is origin potentially trustworthy?", step 3). Whether each browser follows this after a click-through was not checked (see Unresolved).
35	- `crypto.randomUUID()` and `crypto.subtle` require a secure context; `crypto.getRandomValues()` does not, so the page can make op ids without depending on secure-context status. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webcrypto/ (Crypto interface WebIDL).
36	- Cookies are not isolated by port: a host's cookies go to every port on that host. A `__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and still ignores the port. Evidence: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html (Introduction; `__Host-` prefix section).
37	- `localStorage` is per origin ("the `Storage` object associated with window's origin's local storage area"), and an origin is scheme, host and port, so two instances on different ports do not share it. Evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html#dom-localstorage; https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#concept-origin-tuple.
38	- Chrome: a certificate-error bypass is remembered for one week (604800 s), keyed by host (not port), the certificate chain's SHA-256 fingerprint and the error code. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc (`kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds`).
39	- Chrome: an allowed decision is applied to any later request to that host carrying that certificate, not only to top-level navigation. `OnCertError` queries the policy by request host and certificate and continues on `ALLOWED`, with no frame-type check. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/content/browser/ssl/ssl_manager.cc. WebSocket certificate errors reach the same browser-side handler through the network-service client (`services/network/websocket_factory.cc`, https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/b95c2d2c8a7ea8efcec38e091c19bfbeac6af8d1/services/network/websocket_factory.cc). That is an older snapshot, read but not run.
40	- Chrome lets the user proceed past a missing SAN (COMMON_NAME_INVALID), an untrusted authority, a date error, "validity too long" and "self-signed local network". Only the fatal set (contains errors, revoked, invalid, pinned key) or strict enforcement (HSTS-style) blocks it. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/core/ssl_error_options_mask.cc.
41	- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt applies to requests from a public-network page to local or loopback addresses. A page loaded from the LAN address calling its own origin is local-to-local and outside it. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access.
42	- Firefox: a certificate exception pins the presented certificate to host and port, and Firefox shows no prompt for a failed subresource such as `wss`. The page must therefore be loaded (and the exception made) on the same host:port as the socket, which same-origin guarantees. Evidence: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1109773 (comment on exceptions pinning to host/port); https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1187666 (WONTFIX: no dialog for subresources).
43	- Apple (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15 and later): a TLS server certificate must carry the server's name in subjectAltName, and a CN is not trusted. EKU `serverAuth` and validity ≤ 825 days are required only of certificates whose NotBefore is after 2019-07-01. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769. The current certificate's NotBefore is 1975 (above), so as issued only the SAN rule bites. A reissue with today's NotBefore must also carry `serverAuth` and ≤ 825 days, or a manually trusted install is refused.
44	- iOS: a certificate profile installed by hand (downloaded or emailed) needs Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings > "Enable full trust for root certificates" before it is trusted for TLS. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102390.
45	
46	## Unresolved
47	
48	- Whether any browser API lets a page read the certificate of its own connection. If none does, the page's key check proves only what `/info` claims, and §5's relay sentence must be amended for browsers. Not looked up; no source found either way.
49	- Whether Safari (iOS and macOS) applies a click-through exception to `wss://` from the page. WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is still NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, with no fix noted. Its reports date from the CFStream era. Tried: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 and https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 (which says WebKit moved to an NSURLSession WebSocket, behind a flag at the time). Nothing says whether the current implementation honours the exception, and it needs a person's tap in Safari. **This is the question the plan turns on most.** See For the owner.
50	- Whether `fetch` from the page honours the Safari exception. It is expected, since the page itself loaded, but no WebKit source or document was found. Tried: the WebKit bugs above and a web search.
51	- How long Safari (macOS and iOS) remembers a click-through, and whether it survives a relaunch. Tried: web search; no Apple or WebKit source found.
52	- Whether each browser treats a clicked-through page as a secure context in practice (`isSecureContext`, `Secure` cookies). The spec says yes by scheme. No vendor statement was found, and Chrome is known to refuse service-worker registration on certificate errors (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1162772 and a search; a lead only), which shows certificate state can gate features. Not run.
53	- Whether `SameSite=Strict` cookies go on a same-origin `wss` handshake in each browser. The specs imply yes: a same-origin Fetch with credentials included, and schemeful same-site treats `wss` and `https` as the same scheme (https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/qB7DKqxkiaA/m/w0XzGvEyBAAJ, a proposal, not a spec). The rfc6265bis text read did not cover WebSockets, and no browser was run.
54	- Whether a `Secure` cookie can be set from an IP-literal https host with a clicked-through certificate. rfc6265bis leaves "secure connection" to the user agent. Not run.
55	- Whether the URL with `?code=` lands in Safari's global history, tab list or iCloud Tabs before `replaceState` runs, and whether `replaceState` rewrites those. The HTML spec covers only the session-history entry; global history is user-agent behaviour. Mitigated by the single-use code (Settled). Tried: search; no source.
56	- How many parallel HTTP/1.1 connections per host iOS Safari opens, and whether the certificate-warning handshake holds a slot in the pool of 4 until timeout or frees it at once. A lead only: Apple's `URLSessionConfiguration.httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost` is documented as 4 on iOS and 6 on macOS, but that is the app API, not Safari. Not run.
57	- Whether the `<hostname -s>.local` name `mdns-sd` registers matches the Mac's own LocalHostName, which mDNSResponder advertises separately, and so which `.local` name a URL should carry. Not checked.
58	- Whether iOS Safari resolves `<name>.local` and whether Android browsers do. Not searched to a primary source; needs a device.
59	- Whether iOS offers the "full trust" toggle for a self-signed leaf with no `basicConstraints CA:true` (the current certificate is `IsCa::NoCa`). The Apple page speaks of "root certificates" only. Not checked.
60	
61	## For the owner
62	
63	- **Run on a real iPhone (and once in macOS Safari):** open `https://<lan ip>:<port>/` from the current certificate, accept the warning, then in the page check `fetch('/api/v1/info')`, `new WebSocket('wss://…/api/v1/events')`, `isSecureContext`, and whether a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a `fetch` POST is sent on the socket. If all work: the plan takes the click-through as the trust step (decision 1) and may use the cookie (decision 2). If the socket fails: the plan either makes certificate install the trust step (reissue with an IP SAN, `serverAuth`, ≤ 825 days and possibly CA:true, plus the iOS full-trust toggle), or replaces the socket for the page with polling or a `fetch`-streamed event feed on the same path the exception already covers. # Issue #230 facts: a web control surface on the remote port

There was no spike. The tree and primary sources settle everything that
can be checked here. What is left needs a real browser on a device and
a person's tap through the certificate warning. Safari is the only
browser on this Mac, and driving it needs `safaridriver --enable`, an
admin step, so none of it runs here. Line numbers are at 7fe8949.

## Settled

### The tree

- `RemoteRequest` is built in one place, `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:506`). Nothing in `tests/`, `control/` or `client/` names `RemoteRequest` or `RemoteReply` (grep), because `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP. A new request field (cookie, origin, user agent, subprotocol) touches one constructor. Evidence: `grep -rn "RemoteRequest {"` gives only `src/adapters/remote.rs:506`.
- `RemoteReply { status, body, authenticated }` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:389-393`) is built literally 28 times in `src/app.rs` and twice in `src/adapters/remote.rs`. A headers field needs a `Default` or a constructor, or all 30 sites change. Evidence: `grep -c "RemoteReply {"`.
- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` are in `src/adapters/`, not in `ports/`, `model.rs` or `action.rs`, so CLAUDE.md's additive-contract rule ("`src/core/model.rs`, `src/core/action.rs` … and `src/ports/` are the shared contract") does not cover them. Evidence: CLAUDE.md "Extending the contract"; `src/adapters/remote.rs:360,389`.
- The certificate can be reissued over the existing key without changing `spki_sha256`. The SPKI hash is computed from the key alone (`spki_sha256_of_key`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:138-141`), and rcgen signs any params with a loaded key (`KeyPair::from_pem`, `:139,146`; `CertificateParams::self_signed(&self, signing_key)`, rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:154`). `make_identity` always generates a new key (`src/adapters/remote.rs:105`), so a reissue is a new function.
- rcgen 0.14 can carry what a browser or an installed trust needs: `subject_alt_names` with `SanType::IpAddress` and DNS names, `extended_key_usages` with `ServerAuth`, `not_before`/`not_after` and `is_ca`. Evidence: rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:57-64,755,812`; `src/lib.rs:313`.
- rcgen's default validity is notBefore 1975-01-01 to notAfter 4096-01-01, and the current certificate takes both. Evidence: rcgen-0.14.10 `src/certificate.rs:83-84`; `src/adapters/remote.rs:106` (`CertificateParams::new` with no override).
- The current certificate has no subjectAltName, only a CN, and no EKU. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:106-111`.
- `local_address()` always returns IPv4. It binds `0.0.0.0` and connects to `192.0.2.1`, so a URL built from it never needs IPv6 brackets. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`.
- The Bonjour host name is `<hostname -s>.local.` as registered by `mdns-sd` (`src/adapters/bonjour.rs:41-48`, `default_server_name` `src/adapters/remote.rs:304-313`). Whether that matches macOS's own LocalHostName is not checked here (Unresolved).
- A code is single use: the first pairing closes the window. The window also closes after three failures or five minutes. A code left in browser history is dead once used or expired. Evidence: `src/core/remote.rs:46-69` (`Paired` sets `self.pairing = None`).
- The record carries no `last_message`. It exists only on the hook event (`src/ports/events.rs:24`, `src/adapters/hooks.rs:71,196`) and is not on `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`). The card's excerpt is computed in the UI from the transcript for agents (`agent_excerpt`, `src/ui/cards.rs:176-178,558`) and from the pane caption or host title for the other kinds (`src/ui/cards.rs:179-184`). An excerpt on the wire is therefore new work, not a field to expose.
- The watch set is global across the port, capped at 128, least recently read evicted silently. A page that watches one key per listed session can push a headset's keys out. The headset loses only the `changed` events until its next read. Evidence: `docs/remote-client.md:131,254,543`.
- The spec forbids the token in a URL: "sent only as a bearer header … never in a URL" (`docs/remote-client.md:312`) and "keep tokens out of logs, URLs" (`:318`). Both lines name the bearer header, so either cookie or subprotocol transport amends `:312`.
- §5's claim that "a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails" (`docs/remote-client.md:309`) rests on the client sending the `spki_sha256` it saw on the wire. The host checks only what the body says (`remote_pair`, `src/app.rs:3639-3647`), so the claim holds only for a client that can read its own connection's certificate (whether any browser API exposes it: Unresolved).
- The pairing token is base64url with no padding, 43 characters (`src/adapters/remote.rs:340`; `docs/remote-client.md:312`). Its characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _` are all RFC 7230 `tchar`, so it is a valid `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230#section-3.2.6 (tchar includes `-` and `_`).
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114-116`). It is called by `switchboard-remote` (`main.swift:111`) and `BrowserView` (`:106` for a pasted line, `:883`). `ConnectionManager` builds one (`:474`) and uses `invite.addresses.compactMap(Address.init).first` (`:483`), so only the first address is used and a one-element list from a URL is enough. Eight test files under `client/Tests` name `PairingInvite`.

### Browsers and platforms

- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` takes no headers. The handshake is a Fetch with credentials mode `"include"`, so the browser's cookies for the URL go with it. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ ("credentials mode … include"; constructor signature).
- If the page passes a subprotocol and the 101 response does not echo one of them, the browser fails the connection. The host must therefore write `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` in `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) if the token travels that way. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (opening handshake: "covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server").
- Secure contexts are decided by scheme alone: an `https`/`wss` origin is "potentially trustworthy" whatever the certificate's state. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ ("Is origin potentially trustworthy?", step 3). Whether each browser follows this after a click-through was not checked (see Unresolved).
- `crypto.randomUUID()` and `crypto.subtle` require a secure context; `crypto.getRandomValues()` does not, so the page can make op ids without depending on secure-context status. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webcrypto/ (Crypto interface WebIDL).
- Cookies are not isolated by port: a host's cookies go to every port on that host. A `__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and still ignores the port. Evidence: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html (Introduction; `__Host-` prefix section).
- `localStorage` is per origin ("the `Storage` object associated with window's origin's local storage area"), and an origin is scheme, host and port, so two instances on different ports do not share it. Evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html#dom-localstorage; https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#concept-origin-tuple.
- Chrome: a certificate-error bypass is remembered for one week (604800 s), keyed by host (not port), the certificate chain's SHA-256 fingerprint and the error code. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc (`kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds`).
- Chrome: an allowed decision is applied to any later request to that host carrying that certificate, not only to top-level navigation. `OnCertError` queries the policy by request host and certificate and continues on `ALLOWED`, with no frame-type check. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/content/browser/ssl/ssl_manager.cc. WebSocket certificate errors reach the same browser-side handler through the network-service client (`services/network/websocket_factory.cc`, https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/b95c2d2c8a7ea8efcec38e091c19bfbeac6af8d1/services/network/websocket_factory.cc). Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/core/ssl_error_options_mask.cc.
- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt applies to requests from a public-network page to local or loopback addresses. A page loaded from the LAN address calling its own origin is local-to-local and outside it. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access.
- Firefox: a certificate exception pins the presented certificate to host and port, and Firefox shows no prompt for a failed subresource such as `wss`. The page must therefore be loaded (and the exception made) on the same host:port as the socket, which same-origin guarantees. Evidence: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1109773 (comment on exceptions pinning to host/port); https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1187666 (WONTFIX: no dialog for subresources).
- Apple (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15 and later): a TLS server certificate must carry the server's name in subjectAltName, and a CN is not trusted. EKU `serverAuth` and validity ≤ 825 days are required only of certificates whose NotBefore is after 2019-07-01. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769. The current certificate's NotBefore is 1975 (above), so as issued only the SAN rule bites. A reissue with today's NotBefore must also carry `serverAuth` and ≤ 825 days, or a manually trusted install is refused.
- iOS: a certificate profile installed by hand (downloaded or emailed) needs Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings > "Enable full trust for root certificates" before it is trusted for TLS. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102390.

## Unresolved

- Whether any browser API lets a page read the certificate of its own connection. If none does, the page's key check proves only what `/info` claims, and §5's relay sentence must be amended for browsers. Not looked up; no source found either way.
- Whether Safari (iOS and macOS) applies a click-through exception to `wss://` from the page. WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is still NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, with no fix noted. Its reports date from the CFStream era. Tried: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 and https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 (which says WebKit moved to an NSURLSession WebSocket, behind a flag at the time). - How long Safari (macOS and iOS) remembers a click-through, and whether it survives a relaunch. Tried: web search; no Apple or WebKit source found.
- Whether each browser treats a clicked-through page as a secure context in practice (`isSecureContext`, `Secure` cookies). The spec says yes by scheme. 32	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` takes no headers. The handshake is a Fetch with credentials mode `"include"`, so the browser's cookies for the URL go with it. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ ("credentials mode … include"; constructor signature).
33	- If the page passes a subprotocol and the 101 response does not echo one of them, the browser fails the connection. The host must therefore write `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` in `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) if the token travels that way. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (opening handshake: "covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server").
34	- Secure contexts are decided by scheme alone: an `https`/`wss` origin is "potentially trustworthy" whatever the certificate's state. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ ("Is origin potentially trustworthy?", step 3). Whether each browser follows this after a click-through was not checked (see Unresolved).
35	- `crypto.randomUUID()` and `crypto.subtle` require a secure context; `crypto.getRandomValues()` does not, so the page can make op ids without depending on secure-context status. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webcrypto/ (Crypto interface WebIDL).
36	- Cookies are not isolated by port: a host's cookies go to every port on that host. A `__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and still ignores the port. Evidence: https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html (Introduction; `__Host-` prefix section).
37	- `localStorage` is per origin ("the `Storage` object associated with window's origin's local storage area"), and an origin is scheme, host and port, so two instances on different ports do not share it. Evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html#dom-localstorage; https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#concept-origin-tuple.
38	- Chrome: a certificate-error bypass is remembered for one week (604800 s), keyed by host (not port), the certificate chain's SHA-256 fingerprint and the error code. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc (`kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds`).
39	- Chrome: an allowed decision is applied to any later request to that host carrying that certificate, not only to top-level navigation. `OnCertError` queries the policy by request host and certificate and continues on `ALLOWED`, with no frame-type check. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/content/browser/ssl/ssl_manager.cc. WebSocket certificate errors reach the same browser-side handler through the network-service client (`services/network/websocket_factory.cc`, https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/b95c2d2c8a7ea8efcec38e091c19bfbeac6af8d1/services/network/websocket_factory.cc). That is an older snapshot, read but not run.
40	- Chrome lets the user proceed past a missing SAN (COMMON_NAME_INVALID), an untrusted authority, a date error, "validity too long" and "self-signed local network". Only the fatal set (contains errors, revoked, invalid, pinned key) or strict enforcement (HSTS-style) blocks it. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/security_interstitials/core/ssl_error_options_mask.cc.
41	- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt applies to requests from a public-network page to local or loopback addresses. A page loaded from the LAN address calling its own origin is local-to-local and outside it. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access.
42	- Firefox: a certificate exception pins the presented certificate to host and port, and Firefox shows no prompt for a failed subresource such as `wss`. The page must therefore be loaded (and the exception made) on the same host:port as the socket, which same-origin guarantees. Evidence: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1109773 (comment on exceptions pinning to host/port); https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1187666 (WONTFIX: no dialog for subresources).
43	- Apple (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15 and later): a TLS server certificate must carry the server's name in subjectAltName, and a CN is not trusted. EKU `serverAuth` and validity ≤ 825 days are required only of certificates whose NotBefore is after 2019-07-01. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769. The current certificate's NotBefore is 1975 (above), so as issued only the SAN rule bites. A reissue with today's NotBefore must also carry `serverAuth` and ≤ 825 days, or a manually trusted install is refused.
44	- iOS: a certificate profile installed by hand (downloaded or emailed) needs Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings > "Enable full trust for root certificates" before it is trusted for TLS. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102390.
45	
46	## Unresolved
47	
48	- Whether any browser API lets a page read the certificate of its own connection. If none does, the page's key check proves only what `/info` claims, and §5's relay sentence must be amended for browsers. Not looked up; no source found either way.
49	- Whether Safari (iOS and macOS) applies a click-through exception to `wss://` from the page. WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is still NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, with no fix noted. Its reports date from the CFStream era. Tried: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 and https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 (which says WebKit moved to an NSURLSession WebSocket, behind a flag at the time). Nothing says whether the current implementation honours the exception, and it needs a person's tap in Safari. **This is the question the plan turns on most.** See For the owner.
50	- Whether `fetch` from the page honours the Safari exception. It is expected, since the page itself loaded, but no WebKit source or document was found. Tried: the WebKit bugs above and a web search.
51	- How long Safari (macOS and iOS) remembers a click-through, and whether it survives a relaunch. Tried: web search; no Apple or WebKit source found.
52	- Whether each browser treats a clicked-through page as a secure context in practice (`isSecureContext`, `Secure` cookies). The spec says yes by scheme. No vendor statement was found, and Chrome is known to refuse service-worker registration on certificate errors (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1162772 and a search; a lead only), which shows certificate state can gate features. Not run.
53	- Whether `SameSite=Strict` cookies go on a same-origin `wss` handshake in each browser. The specs imply yes: a same-origin Fetch with credentials included, and schemeful same-site treats `wss` and `https` as the same scheme (https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/qB7DKqxkiaA/m/w0XzGvEyBAAJ, a proposal, not a spec). The rfc6265bis text read did not cover WebSockets, and no browser was run.
54	- Whether a `Secure` cookie can be set from an IP-literal https host with a clicked-through certificate. rfc6265bis leaves "secure connection" to the user agent. Not run.
55	- Whether the URL with `?code=` lands in Safari's global history, tab list or iCloud Tabs before `replaceState` runs, and whether `replaceState` rewrites those. The HTML spec covers only the session-history entry; global history is user-agent behaviour. Mitigated by the single-use code (Settled). Tried: search; no source.
56	- How many parallel HTTP/1.1 connections per host iOS Safari opens, and whether the certificate-warning handshake holds a slot in the pool of 4 until timeout or frees it at once. A lead only: Apple's `URLSessionConfiguration.httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost` is documented as 4 on iOS and 6 on macOS, but that is the app API, not Safari. Not run.
57	- Whether the `<hostname -s>.local` name `mdns-sd` registers matches the Mac's own LocalHostName, which mDNSResponder advertises separately, and so which `.local` name a URL should carry. Not checked.
58	- Whether iOS Safari resolves `<name>.local` and whether Android browsers do. Not searched to a primary source; needs a device.
59	- Whether iOS offers the "full trust" toggle for a self-signed leaf with no `basicConstraints CA:true` (the current certificate is `IsCa::NoCa`). The Apple page speaks of "root certificates" only. Not checked.
60	
61	## For the owner
62	
63	- **Run on a real iPhone (and once in macOS Safari):** open `https://<lan ip>:<port>/` from the current certificate, accept the warning, then in the page check `fetch('/api/v1/info')`, `new WebSocket('wss://…/api/v1/events')`, `isSecureContext`, and whether a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a `fetch` POST is sent on the socket. If all work: the plan takes the click-through as the trust step (decision 1) and may use the cookie (decision 2). If the socket fails: the plan either makes certificate install the trust step (reissue with an IP SAN, `serverAuth`, ≤ 825 days and possibly CA:true, plus the iOS full-trust toggle), or replaces the socket for the page with polling or a `fetch`-streamed event feed on the same path the exception already covers. If `isSecureContext` is false: the page avoids `randomUUID` (use `getRandomValues`) and the cookie cannot be `Secure`, which favours the subprotocol token.
64	- **Decision 1, click-through or install:** if click-through, the paired-devices dialog says the warning is the trust step and that the page's key check catches only a wrong host, not an impostor page; the certificate stays as it is. If install, the host serves the certificate before pairing (a fourth pre-pairing path), the identity is reissued over the same key with SANs, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity, and someone owns reissuing when the IP changes.
65	- **Decision 2, cookie or subprotocol:** if cookie, `read_request` reads `Cookie`, `/pair` sets it, the name carries `server_id` to keep two instances apart, and the owner accepts that other HTTPS services on that host receive it (ports are not isolated). If subprotocol, the token lives in page storage readable by any script on the origin, and `respond_upgrade` must echo the value.
66	- **Check `Origin` on the upgrade and on POSTs?** If yes, decide the accepted set (LAN IP, `.local` name, loopback, each with the port). If no, a cookie transport is open to cross-site WebSocket hijacking from another LAN page, and the plan should prefer the subprotocol.
67	- **"Revoked" versus "never paired":** if a new refusal code, it is an additive code from `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3125-3153`). If not, the page keeps a non-secret "paired with server X" marker and infers revocation.
68	- **Scope in the header after pairing:** if a new authenticated endpoint, it is additive and the Swift client can use it too. If not, the header shows the `/pair` reply's scope and may go stale.
69	- **Card excerpt:** if on the wire, it is a new computed field on `SessionView` with a fixture change on both sides, since the record has no `last_message`. If not, the page fetches `last-response` per session as the headset does and spends watch-set slots.
70	- **One QR or two:** if one URL, `PairingInvite.parse` learns URLs (only the first address is used), the README's "Copy invite" text changes, and the JSON stays as a parse fallback. If two, nothing in Swift changes.
71	- **URL host: IP or `.local`:** if `.local`, a certificate exception or SAN binds to that name and survives IP changes. If IP, a new address means a new warning in Chrome; in Firefox a new address is a new host:port.
72	- **Static paths:** if answered on the connection thread, they cost no frame time and no inbox slot. If on the frame, they go through `serve_remote`. Either way, decide whether they get a rate window and whether a page load may hold the unauthenticated pool of 4 (the device run above shows how many connections Safari opens).
73	- **Page logic untested by CI** (no JS harness allowed): if accepted, the host-side tests cover paths, headers and the pairing flow, and the page is checked by hand. If not, the issue's no-dependency rule needs relaxing.

1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.
103	
104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.
137	
138	### The session list and the excerpt
139	
140	- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
141	  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
142	  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
143	  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
144	  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
145	  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
146	  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
147	  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
148	  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
149	  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
150	  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
151	  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
152	  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
153	- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
154	  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
155	  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
156	  `:3116-3118`).
157	- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
158	  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
159	  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
160	  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
161	- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
162	  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
163	  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
164	  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.
165	
166	### Pairing UI and the text paths
167	
168	- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
169	  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
170	  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
171	  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
172	  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
173	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
174	  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
175	  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
176	  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
177	  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
178	  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
179	  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
180	  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
181	- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
182	  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
183	  the payload.
184	- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
185	  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
186	  against a test data dir.
187	
188	### Tests that exist and what extends
189	
190	- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
191	  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
192	  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
193	  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
194	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
195	  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
196	  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
197	  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
198	  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
199	- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
200	  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
201	  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
202	  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
203	  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
204	  only by hand.
205	- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.
206	
207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after

# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes

Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.

## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back

- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
  not to any record.
- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
  address that moves would need another reissue.

## What the code does today, piece by piece

### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)

- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
  (that is a question below, not checked).
- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
  here.

### The router (`src/app.rs`)

- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
  Y").
- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
  new static handler must keep that true.

### The session list and the excerpt

- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
  `:3116-3118`).
- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.

### Pairing UI and the text paths

- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`

  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
  the payload.
- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
  against a test data dir.

### Tests that exist and what extends

- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are

  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
  only by hand.
- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.

  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
  not at the connection thread.
- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
